facts.text: The only hitter of the 1940s to collect 180 hits and score 65 runs or fewer was Luke Appling — and he did it twice (1943: 192 H, 63 R; 1946: 180 H, 59 R).
The only hitter of the 1940s to get 200 hits and 100 walks: Stan Musial, 1949 — 207 H, 107 BB.
The only hitter of the 1940s to collect 230 hits: Stan Musial, 1948 — 230 H.
The only hitter of the 1940s to hit 25+ homers at age 36 or older: Hank Greenberg, 1947 — 25 HR at 36.
The only pitcher of the 1940s to allow 35+ homers and still win 15: Larry Jansen, 1949 — 36 HR allowed, 15-16.
The only hitter of the 1940s to hit 45 doubles and 5 homers or fewer was Lou Boudreau — and he did it twice (1944: 45 2B, 3 HR; 1947: 45 2B, 4 HR).
The only hitter of the 1940s to hit 30+ homers with 15 doubles or fewer: Charlie Keller, 1943 — 31 HR, 15 2B.
The only hitter of the 1940s to hit 25+ homers at age 22 or younger: Ted Williams, 1941 — 37 HR at 22.
The only pitcher of the 1940s to post an ERA under 3.00 and win 7 or fewer (162+ IP): Al Benton, 1942 — 2.90 ERA, 7-13.
The only hitter of the 1940s to hit 25+ homers while batting under .240 (400+ PA): Pat Seerey, 1946 — 26 HR, .225.
The only pitcher of the 1940s to post an ERA under 2.50 with a losing record (25+ starts): Ewell Blackwell, 1946 — 2.45 ERA, 9-13.
The only hitter of the 1940s to bat .400 (400+ PA): Ted Williams, 1941 — .406.
Only two hitters of the 1940s batted .320 at age 36 or older (500+ PA): Bob Johnson (1944: .324 at 38); Luke Appling (1943: .328 at 36).
Only two hitters of the 1940s hit 50 home runs: Ralph Kiner (2×, best 1949: 54 HR); Johnny Mize (1947: 51 HR).
Just three hitters of the 1940s drew 100 walks and struck out 100 times: Eddie Joost (1947: 114 BB, 110 K); Dolph Camilli (1941: 104 BB, 115 K); Charlie Keller (1946: 113 BB, 101 K).
Just four hitters of the 1940s drove in 150 runs: Ted Williams (1949: 159 RBI); Vern Stephens (1949: 159 RBI); Joe DiMaggio (1948: 155 RBI); Hank Greenberg (1940: 150 RBI).

Just four hitters of the 1940s drove in 100 runs with 8 homers or fewer: Dixie Walker (1945: 124 RBI, 8 HR); Bob Elliott (2×, best 1945: 108 RBI, 8 HR); Billy Herman (1943: 100 RBI, 2 HR); Cecil Travis (1941: 101 RBI, 7 HR).
Just three hitters of the 1940s scored 120 runs with 50 RBI or fewer: Eddie Stanky (1945: 128 R, 39 RBI); Snuffy Stirnweiss (1944: 125 R, 43 RBI); Jackie Robinson (1947: 125 R, 48 RBI).
Only two pitchers of the 1940s won 18+ games at age 22 or younger: Bob Feller (2×, best 1940: 27-11 at 21); Ralph Branca (1947: 21-12 at 21).
Only two pitchers of the 1940s won 15 games walking 30 batters or fewer: Tiny Bonham (1942: 21-5, 24 BB); Freddie Fitzsimmons (1940: 16-2, 25 BB).
Only two hitters of the 1940s batted .310 while slugging under .380 (500+ PA): Luke Appling (1948: .314 AVG, .354 SLG); Mickey Witek (1943: .314 AVG, .370 SLG).
George Case stole 30+ bases in 6 straight seasons (1940-45), the longest run of the 1940s.
Hal Newhouser threw 250+ innings in 6 straight seasons (1944-49), the longest run of the 1940s.
The 1945 Washington Senators are the only team of the 1940s with two players at 30+ steals: George Myatt 30, George Case 30.
The 1946 Detroit Tigers are the only team of the 1940s with two players at 150+ strikeouts: Hal Newhouser 275, Virgil Trucks 161, Dizzy Trout 151.
Just three pitchers of the 1940s won 20 and lost 15 in the same season: Bob Feller (1946: 26-15); Johnny Sain (1948: 24-15); Bill Voiselle (1944: 21-16).
Dixie Walker batted .300 or better (500+ PA) in 5 straight seasons (1943-47), the longest run of the 1940s.
Just three hitters of the 1940s grounded into 28+ double plays: Bobby Doerr (1949: 31 GIDP); Jimmy Bloodworth (1943: 29 GIDP); George Kell (1944: 28 GIDP).

Just four hitters of the 1940s batted .330 at age 22 or younger (500+ PA): Ted Williams (2×, best 1941: .406 at 22); Stan Musial (1943: .357 at 22); Pete Reiser (1941: .343 at 22); Richie Ashburn (1948: .333 at 21).
Just three pitchers of the 1940s won 12+ games without a start: Earl Caldwell (1946: 13-4, 0 GS); Joe Page (1949: 13-8, 0 GS); Johnny Murphy (1943: 12-4, 0 GS).
Just four pitchers of the 1940s threw 8+ shutouts: Mort Cooper (1942: 10 SHO); Bob Feller (1946: 10 SHO); Bob Lemon (1948: 10 SHO); Hal Newhouser (1945: 8 SHO).

Just four pitchers of the 1940s struck out 6.5+ per nine innings (162+ IP): Hal Newhouser (2×, best 1946: 8.5 K/9, 275 K); Bob Feller (3×, best 1946: 8.4 K/9, 348 K); Johnny Vander Meer (2×, best 1941: 8.0 K/9, 202 K); Allie Reynolds (1943: 6.8 K/9, 151 K).

Just four pitchers of the 1940s posted an ERA under 2.00 (162+ IP): Spud Chandler (1943: 1.64 ERA in 253.0 IP); Mort Cooper (1942: 1.78 ERA in 278.2 IP); Hal Newhouser (2×, best 1945: 1.81 ERA in 313.1 IP); Max Lanier (1943: 1.94 ERA in 213.1 IP).
11 hitters played a full season without a single home run (600+ PA) in the 1940s (13 seasons). The most extreme: Johnny Pesky, 1947 — 0 HR in 719 PA.
Lowest average by any 100-RBI hitter of the 1940s: Dolph Camilli, 1942 — .252 with 109 RBI.
Most strikeouts by a .300 hitter of the 1940s: Jimmie Foxx, 1941 — 103 K while batting .300.
Most steals by a 30-homer hitter of the 1940s: Joe Gordon, 1940 — 18 SB with 30 HR.
Most home runs per RBI of the 1940s: Ralph Kiner, 1949 — 54 HR but only 127 RBI.
Fewest strikeouts by a 25-homer hitter of the 1940s: Tommy Holmes, 1945 — 9 K with 28 HR.
Highest average by a hitter with 3 homers or fewer: Harry Walker, 1947 — .363 with 1 HR.
Most walks by a sub-.240 hitter of the 1940s: Roy Cullenbine, 1947 — 137 BB while batting .224.
Most RBI per home run among 100-RBI seasons: Billy Herman, 1943 — 100 RBI on 2 HR.
Most wins by a pitcher with an ERA over 5.00: Elden Auker, 1941 — 14-15 with a 5.50 ERA.
Fewest wins by a qualified pitcher with an ERA under 3.00: Al Benton, 1942 — 7-13 despite a 2.90 ERA.
Most strikeouts by a pitcher with a losing record: Bobo Newsom, 1941 — 175 K, 12-20.
Most losses by a pitcher with an ERA under 3.50: Nate Andrews, 1943 — 14-20 with a 2.57 ERA.
Fewest strikeouts by a 20-game winner of the 1940s: Rip Sewell, 1943 — 65 K, 21-9.
Most innings in a season without a complete game: Joe Page, 1947 — 141.1 IP, 0 CG.
Most home runs allowed in a season this decade: Murry Dickson, 1948 — 39 HR allowed, 12-16.
9 teams of the 1940s won 100 games; the best record was the 1942 Cardinals at 106-48.
9 pitchers threw 300 innings in the 1940s (13 seasons). The most extreme: Bob Feller, 1946 — 371.1 IP.
13 pitchers walked 130+ batters in the 1940s (16 seasons). The most extreme: Bob Feller, 1941 — 194 BB.
Ted Williams hit 25+ home runs in 4 straight seasons (1946-49), the longest run of the 1940s.
Ted Williams drove in 100+ runs in 4 straight seasons (1946-49), the longest run of the 1940s.
Oldest player of the 1940s to hit 25 home runs: Hank Greenberg, age 36 in 1947 — 25 HR.
Oldest player of the 1940s to bat .330 (500+ PA): Rip Radcliff, age 34 in 1940 — .342.
Oldest player of the 1940s to drive in 100 runs: Bob Johnson, age 38 in 1944 — 106 RBI.
Youngest player of the 1940s to steal 30 bases: Richie Ashburn, age 21 in 1948 — 32 SB.
Oldest player of the 1940s to steal 30 bases: Wally Moses, age 32 in 1943 — 56 SB.
Oldest player of the 1940s to win 20 games: Spud Chandler, age 38 in 1946 — 20-8.
Oldest player of the 1940s to strike out 150: Whit Wyatt, age 33 in 1941 — 176 K.
Oldest player of the 1940s to post a qualified ERA under 2.75: Ted Lyons, age 41 in 1942 — 2.10 ERA.
4 hitter-seasons of the 1940s ended on exactly 29 home runs, one short of 30 — among them Vern Stephens (1948), Bill Nicholson (1943), Joe Gordon (1947).
7 teams of the 1940s had two players at 30+ home runs; the biggest pairing was the 1947 New York Giants — Johnny Mize 51, Willard Marshall 36, Walker Cooper 35.
Most home runs in the 1940s by a hitter who never led the majors in a season: Joe Gordon, 181.
Most hits of the 1940s: Lou Boudreau, 1578.
Most stolen bases of the 1940s: George Case, 285.
Most strikeouts by a hitter in the 1940s: Bill Nicholson, 708.
Most triples of the 1940s: Stan Musial, 108.
Most RBI of the 1940s: Bob Elliott, 903.
Most losses of the 1940s: Dutch Leonard, 123 — and 122 wins.
1948 had 14 25-homer hitters, the most of any season in the 1940s.
1944 had just 2 25-homer hitters, the fewest of any season in the 1940s.
1940 had 29 .300 hitters (500+ PA), the most of any season in the 1940s.
1943 had just 11 .300 hitters (500+ PA), the fewest of any season in the 1940s.
1948 had 16 100-RBI hitters, the most of any season in the 1940s.
1943 had just 6 100-RBI hitters, the fewest of any season in the 1940s.
1945 had 3 30-steal players, the most of any season in the 1940s.
1940 had just 1 30-steal players, the fewest of any season in the 1940s.
1940 had 3 200-hit seasons, the most of any season in the 1940s.
1941 had just 1 200-hit seasons, the fewest of any season in the 1940s.
1946 had 7 20-game winners, the most of any season in the 1940s.
1941 had just 4 20-game winners, the fewest of any season in the 1940s.
1946 had 5 150-strikeout pitchers, the most of any season in the 1940s.
1945 had just 1 150-strikeout pitchers, the fewest of any season in the 1940s.
10 teams of the 1940s lost 100 games; the worst was the 1941 Phillies at 43-111.
Best run differential of the 1940s: the 1942 Yankees, +294 (801 scored, 507 allowed).
3 hitter-seasons of the 1940s ended on a .299 average, one point short of .300 — among them Sid Gordon (1948), Mickey Vernon (1941), Bobby Estalella (1945).
2 hitter-seasons of the 1940s ended on exactly 99 RBI, one short of 100 — among them Chet Laabs (1942), Hank Sauer (1949).
2 hitter-seasons of the 1940s ended on exactly 199 hits, one short of 200 — among them Lou Boudreau (1948), Jeff Heath (1941).
8 pitchers won 15+ games at age 37 or older in the 1940s. The most extreme: Rip Sewell, 1944 — 21-12 at 37.
12 hitters posted a .400 on-base with 5 homers or fewer (500+ PA) in the 1940s (20 seasons). The most extreme: Eddie Stanky, 1946 — .436 OBP, 0 HR.
Worst run differential of the 1940s: the 1945 Phillies, -317 (548 scored, 865 allowed).
6 hitters drew more walks than hits (400+ PA) in the 1940s (8 seasons). The most extreme: Roy Cullenbine, 1947 — 137 BB, 104 H.
11 pitchers lost 20 games in the 1940s (12 seasons). The most extreme: Hugh Mulcahy, 1940 — 13-22.
34 hitters hit 12+ triples and more triples than homers in the 1940s (40 seasons). The most extreme: Dale Mitchell, 1949 — 23 3B, 3 HR.
6 hitters hit 25+ homers with more homers than strikeouts in the 1940s (10 seasons). The most extreme: Tommy Holmes, 1945 — 28 HR, 9 K.
10 hitters struck out 15 times or fewer in a full season (600+ PA) in the 1940s (16 seasons). The most extreme: Tommy Holmes, 1945 — 9 K in 713 PA.
8 pitchers posted a WHIP of 1.05 or lower (162+ IP) in the 1940s. The most extreme: Mort Cooper, 1942 — 0.99 WHIP in 278.2 IP.
16 hitters posted an on-base 130+ points above the batting average (500+ PA) in the 1940s (30 seasons). The most extreme: Roy Cullenbine, 1947 — .224 AVG, .401 OBP.

method: Every fact is a predicate evaluated over every hitter-season and pitcher-season in the decade, pulled in full from the MLB Stats API (the official record). Nothing is recalled or estimated; the rows that satisfy each rule are stored with it.

'Only', 'two' and 'three/four' claims are exact counts across the complete pull. Where a rule uses a plate-appearance or innings floor instead of a league qualification bar, the floor is stated in the fact so the claim is reproducible.
Thresholds are era-aware (strikeouts, saves and home runs meant different things in 1925 and 1995) and are recorded in the file.
Rules built from plain comparisons carry a Stathead Season Finder spec with the same filters and year range, for independent re-checking on the subscription.
